📥 媒体下载（封面 / 视频 / 图文图片）

默认关闭。开启后会在爬取的同时把媒体文件下载到本地，按帖子聚合存放：

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="# 命令行开关

uv run main.py --platform xhs --type detail --specified_id <帖子URL或ID> --get_media true

uv run main.py --platform xhs --type detail --specified_id < 帖子URL或ID > --get_media true

# 或在 config/base_config.py 中设置 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA = True

落盘结构 （ SAVE_DATA_PATH 为空时落在 data/ 下）：

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="data/xhs/media/{帖子ID}/

├── cover.jpg # 封面

├── video.mp4 # 视频（B站为 DASH 合流产物）

├── cover.jpg # 封面

├── video.mp4 # 视频（B站为 DASH 合流产物）

├── 001.jpg # 图文帖的图片

└── 001_live.mp4 # 对应图片的实况随附视频（有实况时）

支持平台 ：小红书、抖音、快手、B站、微博。贴吧与知乎的数据结构中没有媒体字段，暂不支持。

实况照片（Live Photo） ：抖音和小红书统一由 config/base_config.py 中的 DOWNLOAD_LIVE_PHOTO 控制，默认 True ，仅在 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA 开启时生效。设为 False 后只保存静态图，普通视频下载不受影响。实况视频与静态图使用相同的原始图片序号（如 001.jpg / 001_live.mp4 ），缺失媒体时保留序号空位。这里保存的是独立图片与随附视频，不合成手机相册的 Live Photo，也不转换为 GIF。小红书 Web 返回的实况视频可能自带水印，下载会保留该视频的原始内容。

安装 ffmpeg 后可走 DASH 路径获取最高画质（音视频分轨下载后无损合流）；未安装时自动降级为 mp4 直链，产物名为 video-durl.mp4 以便区分

清晰度由 config/bilibili_config.py 的 BILI_QN 控制（默认 80 = 1080p）；未登录或权限不足时若高清取流被拒，会自动逐档降级到实际可下载的清晰度

媒体下载失败只记录日志，不会中断爬取

已存在的文件会被跳过；需要重新下载时删掉对应目录即可

🖥️ WebUI 可视化操作界面

MediaCrawler 提供了基于 Web 的可视化操作界面，无需命令行也能轻松使用爬虫功能。

开发时需要同时启动后端 API 服务和前端 Vite 开发服务器：

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="# 终端 1：启动 API 服务器（默认端口 8080）

uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port 8080 --reload

# 终端 2：启动前端开发服务器

npm run dev # 默认在 5173 端口启动，并代理 /api 到 8080"> # 终端 1：启动 API 服务器（默认端口 8080）

uv run uvicorn api.main:app --port 8080 --reload

# 终端 2：启动前端开发服务器

npm run dev # 默认在 5173 端口启动，并代理 /api 到 8080

启动成功后，访问 http://localhost:5173/ 即可打开 WebUI 界面。

首次打开会进行环境检测（调用 /api/env/check ），请确保后端服务已启动。如果检测失败，可点击「跳过检测」临时跳过。

Paperclip is the app people use to manage AI agents for work.

Open-source orchestration for teams of AI agents.

If OpenClaw is an employee , Paperclip is the company .

Paperclip is a Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents to run a business. Bring your own agents, assign goals, and track work and costs from one dashboard. Choose models and harnesses per agent while keeping your team's tasks, skills, permissions, and history in one place.

It looks like a task manager. Under the hood: org charts, budgets, governance, goal alignment, and agent coordination.

Manage business goals, not pull requests.

Define the goal

"Build the #1 AI note-taking app to $1M MRR."

Hire the team

CEO, CTO, engineers, designers, marketers — any bot, any provider.

Review strategy. Set budgets. Hit go. Monitor from the dashboard.

If it can receive a heartbeat, it's hired.

Custom processes, HTTP endpoints, and external adapter packages extend the roster. See the adapter overview for setup and capabilities.

Paperclip is right for you if

✅ You want to build autonomous AI organizations

✅ You coordinate many different agents (OpenClaw, Codex, Claude, Cursor) toward a common goal

✅ You have 20 simultaneous Claude Code terminals open and lose track of what everyone is doing

✅ You want agents running autonomously 24/7 , but still want to audit work and chime in when needed

✅ You want to monitor costs and enforce budgets

✅ You want a process for managing agents that feels like using a task manager

✅ You want to manage your autonomous businesses from your phone

The four pillars

Four things have to work for an organization of AI agents to actually produce: the tasks, the org, the training, and the infrastructure. Paperclip is built around exactly those four pillars.

What it covers

Agentic Task Manager — Declare intent. Agents work. You verify the output.

Everyone, daily

Tasks, approvals & review gates · proactive agent coworkers · auditable routines & workflows · verify from diffs, screenshots & tests

Org Chart for Agents — Roles, permissions & boundaries for humans and agents.

Mixed human + agent org chart · responsibilities, delegation, specialization · governance: who can do what · scoped secrets & company boundaries · connection permissions & responsible-user identities

Agent Employee Training — Design, train & evaluate your AI employees.

Skill Studio & shared org-wide skills · evals & saved test runs · active learning loops & quality metrics · performance reviews for agents · saved test inputs · skill version history & restore · reusable team templates

<a id="user-content-prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink:

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

" href="#prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness">

Documentation •

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as variables ( prompt-as-a-variable ) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls ( programmatic tool /sub-agent calling ) inside a persistent REPL.

The Continual Harness stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer:

curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh

On Windows, install from PowerShell:

irm https: // app.primeintellect.ai / prime - agent / install.ps1 | iex

The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation.

Why Prime Agent

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

Everything is programmatic: a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

Subagents are built in: rlm.spawn(...) spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.

The harness can improve: /refine reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Skills are executable: skills are importable Python packages, and the built-in skill creator can turn recurring workflows into project or personal skills.

Sessions run in the background: daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects and can be reattached later.

Agents communicate directly: running agents can exchange messages and orchestrate one another without routing everything through the user.

Long tasks keep moving: automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.

Connect Slack from /mcp or run /mcp login slack inside Prime Agent to search

your workspace and use Slack tools. See the Slack connector guide

for OAuth setup and troubleshooting.

Google Drive and Google Sheets

Connect Google's official Drive and Sheets MCP servers with your own Google

OAuth client: add them to mcpServers with clientId , clientSecret ,

callbackPort , and scopes , then run /mcp login <name> . See the

Google Drive and Google Sheets guide for the

Google Cloud setup and the tool mapping.

Clipboard over SSH and tmux

Prime Agent uses the local clipboard tool (such as pbcopy ) when available. In tmux it asks the attached tmux client to forward a clipboard buffer if that client advertises the Ms capability. This works with tmux's default set-clipboard external , unlike application-origin OSC 52. Without tmux, remote copies request delivery using OSC 52. Terminal requests cannot confirm that your local clipboard changed, so Prime Agent reports them as unconfirmed.

Nested tmux servers and terminals may still block delivery. An outer tmux with set-clipboard external can reject the inner server's OSC 52. In that case, run tmux set -s set-clipboard on on the outer server, or use native terminal selection (Shift-drag in most terminals; Option-drag in iTerm2) followed by Cmd-C. macOS Terminal.app does not support OSC 52; iTerm2 requires its “Applications in terminal may access clipboard” setting.

Custom certificate authorities

HTTPS requests trust your operating system's trust store together with the bundled Mozilla roots. For servers behind a custom CA, point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS at a PEM bundle of your CA certificates — the same variable the Node/TypeScript build honors:

export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/your-ca.pem

Each transport reads the variable once when its first client is initialized. The background daemon keeps the environment it started with, so run prime-agent shutdown after changing it.

Getting Started

Start Prime Agent from the repository or directory you want it to work in:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="cd /path/to/project

prime-agent"> cd /path/to/project

On first launch, run /login to choose a subscription or API-key provider. Prime Agent works in the current directory and can run commands and modify files there. Use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore.

π RuView is a WiFi sensing platform that turns radio signals into spatial intelligence.

Every WiFi router already fills your space with radio waves. When people move, breathe, or even sit still, they disturb those waves in measurable ways. RuView captures these disturbances using Channel State Information (CSI) from low-cost ESP32 sensors and turns them into actionable data: who's there, what they're doing, and whether they're okay.

What it senses:

Presence and occupancy — detect people through walls, count them, track entries and exits

Vital signs — breathing rate and heart rate, contactless, while sleeping or sitting

Activity recognition — walking, sitting, gestures, falls — from temporal CSI patterns

Environment mapping — RF fingerprinting identifies rooms, detects moved furniture, spots new objects

Camera-free pose — estimate 17 body keypoints from WiFi CSI

Built-in model workflow — record CSI, train models, load RVF files, and switch LoRA profiles

The AI-Powered Life Operating System

LifeOS-8.761.0-release.mp4

LifeOS is a General Purpose AI Harness for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

And because it has your full context, it makes everything you do more efficient and effective, from building apps, to starting a business, to creative projects… basically anything .

The whole system works on one central concept: moving from your Current State to your Ideal State — in pursuit of Euphoric Surprise.

⭐ If LifeOS is useful to you, star the repo

Stars help more people find the project and keep it moving. It takes one click.

⚠️ Your Security Is Your Responsibility

LifeOS is fundamentally one person's personal AI harness, published as-is, and it is constantly in flux: security features are added, enhanced, removed, modified and adjusted from release to release. The security of any LifeOS component, and of the system as a whole, is not guaranteed. Responsibility for the security of your system is yours, not the LifeOS authors' or contributors'.

Before anything is installed, the installer asks: "Do you understand that you are responsible for the security of your own system and that we are not responsible?" It goes ahead only if you answer yes. See SECURITY.md .

Give it to your AI. LifeOS is installed by an AI, so the install is just a prompt. Paste this into your AI coding harness — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Hermes, or any capable agent — and it does the whole setup for you:

Read https://ourlifeos.ai/install and install LifeOS for me.

Your AI reads the install page and walks the setup, asking permission before it touches anything.

Prefer the terminal? There's a one-line shortcut for Claude Code on macOS/Linux:

curl -fsSL https://ourlifeos.ai/install.sh | bash

Either path needs a capable AI coding harness — we build and run on Claude Code — and bun .

Core Components

The unique features — the parts you won't find anywhere else. Anything a good harness already provides on its own (built-in subagents, for example) isn't listed; this is only what LifeOS adds. See them live and click through on ourlifeos.ai .

LifeOS ships 97 public skills, from research, security, writing and art to video, publishing and your home. Browse them all on the site.

Browse all skills →

How is LifeOS different from using an AI harness on its own?

Your harness gives you raw capability. LifeOS is the layer on top that makes it yours — a system that knows your goals, people, and context, and keeps working toward them:

Persistent memory — Your DA remembers past sessions, decisions, and learnings

Custom skills — Specialized capabilities for the things you do most

Your context — Goals, contacts, preferences—all available without re-explaining

Intelligent routing — Say "research this" and the right workflow triggers automatically

Self-improvement — The system modifies itself based on what it learns

Your harness is the engine. LifeOS is everything else that makes it your car.

What harness does LifeOS run on?

Any high-end one. LifeOS is harness-agnostic by design — it's built on universal primitives (hooks, skills, context files, agentic routing), not one vendor's features. The code is TypeScript and Bash, and the core ideas — TELOS, the Algorithm, skills, memory — port to any capable agent.

Daniel builds and runs it on Claude Code , so that's the most-tested path today. But LifeOS isn't locked to it, and it's designed to run wherever your AI does.

How is this different from fabric?

Fabric is a collection of AI prompts (patterns) for specific tasks. It's focused on what to ask AI .

LifeOS is infrastructure for how your DA operates —memory, skills, routing, context, self-improvement. They're complementary. Many LifeOS users integrate Fabric patterns into their skills.

Back up first — Before any upgrade: cp -r ~/.claude ~/.claude-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

USER/ is safe — Your customizations in USER/ are never touched by the installer or upgrades

Settings merge, not overwrite — The installer only updates identity and version fields; your hooks, statusline, and custom config are preserved

Git-backed — Version control everything, roll back when needed

History is preserved — Your DA's memory survives mistakes

DA can fix it — Your DA helped build it, it can help repair it

Re-install — Run the installer again; it detects existing installations and merges intelligently

WeatherNext 2

This repo contains the code for WeatherNext 2 (WN2), the global, medium-range

atmospheric and cyclone forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind and

Google Research.

It also contains code for prior generation models

Accessing Forecast Data Feeds

If you are interested in directly accessing daily data feeds of WN2 model

outputs rather than running the model yourself, we provide them across multiple

Google Cloud

(including Earth Engine, BigQuery, and Vertex AI).

WeatherLab (including cyclone tracks).

OpenMeteo (including an API and interactive builder).

Model Guide & Documentation: Google Developers WeatherNext Guide

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper: Operational tropical cyclone forecasting

FGN/WN2 Technical Report: Skillful joint probabilistic weather

forecasting from marginals

(arXiv:2506.10772)

WeatherNext 2 Blog Post: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model

WeatherNext Cyclones Blog Post: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones

Older Models

This repository serves as the primary home for the WeatherNext family models.

Alongside WN2, this repository also hosts the code and documentation for our

legacy and specialized models:

WeatherNext Graph : Deterministic

medium-range weather forecasting using graph neural networks. Published as

WeatherNext Gen : Diffusion-based ensemble

forecasting for medium-range weather. Published as GenCast.

Provided Pretrained Models

This repository provides code to run the different versions of WeatherNext 2 and

WeatherNext Cyclones. The only difference between them is that WN2 can also

predict 100m wind. In particular, WN2 also forecasts cyclones with the exact

same algorithm as WN Cyclones. Their weights are different due to independent

training runs.

WeatherNext 2

WeatherNext2_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution (~30km).

Fine-tuned on ECMWF HRES data and designed to be initialized directly from

operational HRES initial conditions rather than ERA5 reanalysis. Trained on

data through 2024. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNext2_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones - models which reproduce the results in paper

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution. The

model that ran live during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, publicly

referred to as FNV3 (NHC's postprocessed version was called GDMI). Trained

on data through 2024. The paper appendix contains a partial evaluation of

2025 in NHC basins for this model checkpoint, and how the tracker

improvement in September 2025 improved results. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2024. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2023. Trained on data through 2022. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones Mini

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024 : 1° resolution. A lightweight version

suitable for lower memory and compute constraints (e.g., local testing or

single TPUs or GPUs). Not expected to match the performance of the larger

versions. Forecasts the same things as WeatherNext2_<2025, including

cyclones. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights file:

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023 : As above, but only trained on data through

2022. Corresponding weights file: WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023.npz .

Evaluation results for WeatherNextCyclones_Mini can be found in the appendix

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper .

Quick Start Guide

The easiest way to get started with WeatherNext 2 is by running our interactive

Colab Notebook , which can be opened from

Colaboratory .

This notebook defaults to WeatherNext Cyclones Mini, which we recommend running

using the v5e-1 runtime, available for free as a Colab runtime. However, the

notebook can also be used to run the other models enumerated above (but these

will require a v5p accelerator).

In general, we recommend running WeatherNext 2 on TPU where possible, since its

implementation has been optimised for it. However, if choosing to run on GPU,

the attention implementation must be switched, as shown in the demo notebook.

The non-Mini models require H100 for sufficient VRAM. The Mini models should

manage inference on a P100.

Pre-trained weights and sample data are available on our Google Cloud

Inside the notebook, you will learn how to:

Automatically load the required model weights from our storage bucket.

Load initial state weather data (e.g., HRES initial conditions).

Initialize the WN2 (FGN) architecture.

Run auto-regressive rollout steps to generate a forecast prediction.

Visualize the outputs (e.g., temperature, wind speed, geopotential height).

Run the direct tracker on model outputs to obtain track data for cyclones.

Compute the training loss on model predictions and targets, and take a

gradient step.

Installation

This is research code provided as-is for the purpose of running and

experimenting with the published models. There are no guarantees of API

stability and future updates may introduce breaking changes without notice. We

recommend pinning to a specific release.

pip install git+https://github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext.git@v0.3.0

Model Weights

To run WeatherNext 2 or WeatherNext Cyclones, you will need to download the

pre-trained model weights. You can access the weights on Google Cloud

Code-Graph-RAG

Code-Graph-RAG parses a multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, sharpened by compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where available, builds a knowledge graph of its structure in an embedded graph database that needs no server, and lets you query, edit, and optimise that code in plain English. It works across a monorepo of mixed languages under one unified graph schema.

1. Index: cgr start --update-graph parses a repository into a knowledge graph (sped up)

2. Ask: cgr start answers questions and edits code, grounded in that graph

Latest News 🔥

Rust Upgrade : Updated Rust to version 1.99.1-slim-trixie.

Signature Functionality : Added support for reading and writing JavaScript headers for change signatures, including the ability to change the signature of JavaScript functions or methods.

macOS Compatibility : The build now leaves macOS-14 support.

See NEWS.md for the full history.

What It Does

Point Code-Graph-RAG at a repository and it reads every source file, extracts functions, classes, methods, modules, and the relationships between them, and stores the result as an interconnected graph. Once the graph exists you can:

Ask questions about the codebase in natural language and get answers grounded in the real structure.

Retrieve the actual source of any function, class, or method by name or by intent.

Edit code through the agent with AST-based surgical patching and a diff preview before anything changes.

Optimise code against language best practices or your own coding standards.

Find dead code by walking call and reference edges from entry points.

Search and rewrite structurally by AST pattern with ast-grep.

Overlay runtime behaviour: trace a test run (or pull production eBPF profiles) with cgr trace and merge the calls that actually happened into the graph, exposing dispatch that static analysis cannot see.

How It Works

The system has two components:

Multi-language parser. A Tree-sitter based parser reads the codebase and ingests functions, classes, methods, modules, and their relationships into the graph under a single language-agnostic schema. Where a toolchain is available, compiler-grade frontends layer exact facts on top (libclang for C/C++, go/types for Go, and opt-in Roslyn, javac and Jedi for C#, Java and Python), and dynamic tracing merges calls observed at runtime. Tree-sitter stays the backbone: a trace only sees code that ran, and a compiler frontend only covers what its toolchain can build.

RAG system ( codebase_rag/ ). An interactive CLI that turns natural language into Cypher queries, retrieves matching code, and drives AI-powered editing and optimisation.

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response"> Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response

The graph is stored in an embedded SQLite file by default. Memgraph and Neo4j are opt-in backends that run the same Cypher; Graph Backends compares them.

See the Architecture Overview and Graph Schema for the full picture.

Supported Languages

Python, TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Lua, Dart, and Julia are fully supported. Scala is in development, and Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Bash, and Nix have structural support (modules, functions, classes where the language has them, and imports) through the pluggable ast-grep tier. See the Language Support matrix for per-language capabilities.

Installation

pipx install "code-graph-rag[treesitter-full,ast-grep,semantic]""> # with uv (recommended)

T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

Installation

T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

Command line

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest instead.

Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

Windows ( winget )

winget install T3Tools.T3Code

Windows ( scoop )

scoop install extras/t3code

macOS (Homebrew)

brew install --cask t3-code

Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

yay -S t3code-bin

yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

Nix (nixpkgs)

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

The package is maintained in nixpkgs

and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.

Developer-first, knowledge infrastructure for AI, alternative to expensive enterprise platforms.

Ingest your enterprise data, extract what matters, build a Context Graph and knowledge graph (KG), and run graph analytics and causal reasoning over all of it, with full decision provenance baked in. Explainable, traceable, and trustworthy by design.

Context Management · Knowledge Modeling · Deterministic Reasoning · Ontology Management · Decision Intelligence · End-to-End Traceability

English · Deutsch · Français · Español · Italiano · Português · العربية · اردو · हिन्दी · 中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Knowledge Explorer · Context Graphs · Reasoning Engine · Decision Intelligence · Ontology Hub

▶ Watch the full platform walkthrough

Most AI agents run on embeddings, not meaning: similarity scores with no structure, no relationships, and no way to explain why a result came back.

Semantica is the semantic/context layer underneath your LLM, vector store, and agent framework: deterministic infrastructure (no LLM required for graph construction, reasoning, or provenance; where an LLM is used, it's optional and vendor-neutral, every major provider supported, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and more, via semantica.llms ) that turns fragmented enterprise data into a structured, queryable Context Graph and knowledge graph that carries the business context, not just the data structure. Ontologies and controlled vocabularies (OWL, SHACL, SKOS) make what an entity means to your business, its definitions, relationships, and rules, as explicit as the data itself, not just its embedding.

Decision provenance and audit trails aren't the product. They fall out of that structure for free, and in domains a regulator can question, the same structure that makes your agent smarter also gives you a straight answer to "why."

System-level explainability, not foundation-model explainability. Semantica doesn't expose or reconstruct what happens inside the LLM: its internal reasoning stays opaque, like it does for any external system. Semantica explains what's outside the model: the context fed in, the decision produced, its provenance, relevant relationships, applied policies, and the full execution trail.

Who it's for:

AI/ML platform teams shipping agents that make consequential decisions and need structured, queryable context, not just a vector index

Enterprise data teams on Databricks, Snowflake, or SAP turning tables already in the lakehouse or warehouse into a governed, lineage-tracked knowledge graph, without exporting to a third-party SaaS

Compliance, risk, and audit teams who need a straight answer to "why did the AI do that?" in a format a regulator accepts

Regulated enterprises (finance, healthcare, legal, government, defense) that can't ship a black box or hand their data to someone else's SaaS to get one

Platform and infra engineers who want the KG, reasoning, and provenance stack self-hosted and swappable, not locked to one vendor's backend

Data and knowledge engineers building a KG from messy, multi-source data, where conflicting facts get flagged and duplicates get merged, not silently overwritten

What Semantica Gives You

Context Graphs: A structured, queryable graph of everything your agent knows, decides, and reasons about

Decision Intelligence: Every decision is a first-class object: traceable, searchable by precedent, and causally linked

AI Governance & Ontology: SHACL constraints, conflict detection, compliance rules, OWL generation, and SKOS vocabularies, all with a visual editor

Full Auditability: W3C PROV-O provenance on every fact, exportable to JSON, CSV, or RDF

Deterministic Reasoning: Forward chaining, Rete network, Datalog, and SPARQL, with fully explainable paths, not black boxes

Knowledge Pipeline: Multi-source ingestion, entity-aware chunking, NER/relation/event extraction, and graph construction, with semantic dedup and provenance-preserving merges built in

Graph Analytics: Centrality, community detection, link prediction, and shortest-path queries over the graph you just built

items.summary: Elon Musk is about to learn how much America hates him（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Swipe for next article

E lon Musk, the “First Tech Bro”, has just found out the hard way that a spend of nearly half a billion dollars and control of a major social media platform cannot always change the political weather. The grand iconoclast tried to make light of the Republican’s midterms catastrophe, posting early on Wednesday that his “election-interfering space lasers didn’t work”. A post telling followers to “Vote red (Republican) today” also, rather sheepishly, disappeared.

Musk is not a man who relishes failure. His spending went to a slew of candidates who failed to get elected in Texas, now the epicentre of his companies’ operations.

For a man whose wealth is estimated at more than $800bn, spending nearly half a billion dollars in campaign donations is surely loose change. But the money was spent for a purpose beyond ideological alignment – Musk has an on-off relationship with Donald Trump, but one which has advanced his interests strategically. And how. Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX slumped following the US midterm elections, wiping out more than $100bn in combined market value.

Elon Musk is now in trouble. In essence, two sides of the Musk sphere of interest have taken a battering. The first is his position as America’s most powerful “tech bro” power broker, a man who could shape the direction of politics and policy towards companies like his Starlink and SpaceX entities. He was outdone by the more raw democratic force of voters disillusioned by Trump over the economy and the Iran war – and in many parts of the electoral map, also anxious about the impact of massive data centres to power the next stages of frontier technology.

The second is that it has laid bare how closely entwined his businesses are with the American state – businesses that rely on a steady flow of regulatory permissions, subsidies and support at the state and federal level to continue their extraordinary growth trajectory and power the next stages of artificial intelligence.

While Democrats need to be wary of leaning too hard into their technophobic wing, there will be a correction from the “anything goes” era when tech titans were largely able to slice their way through opposition or controls.

Government business has always accounted for a large amount of Musk’s revenue, and his empire is entangled with modern US military power. That will not change. But it will face closer inspection as to the consequences. The recent controversy over slowing his Starlink satellite network in Ukraine reminded us that Musk enables a large amount of data flow to support the battlefields of Ukraine. This will surely interest lawmakers. Last month, Senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat from California, called for an investigation into Musk after reports of Starlink blinking out in Ukraine emerged.

Even the “trad” end of the Musk empire – Tesla manufacturing and “robotaxis” – needs huge access to energy infrastructure and computational power. That is why Musk wants to build out his own supporting web of semiconductor companies and data centres , which have also become the focus of protests in the midterms over impacts on electricity and water usage. That has blended classically progressive opinion, which has grown more AI-sceptical in reaction as the unaccountable might of major tech entrepreneurs has increased, and more grassroots concerns about the impact of galloping AI innovations on jobs.

But it is his period as “efficiency tsar” at the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) that could come back to haunt him most. His actual work produced a mixed record at best – and his awkwardly competitive relationship with Trump (and short attention span) meant that it concluded relatively quickly after four months. But that stint did give him a vast amount of information and data, which competitors and critics reckon has given him and his companies a lopsided advantage.

The question of what happened to the information and access acquired during his time in government is now open to a lot more scrutiny in Congress – which can hold hearings, subpoena company bosses and explore the relations between key companies and government contracts and departments. Trump, just before the midterms, said he would be willing to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and allies, including Musk , if Democrats won enough seats to take control of the House and Senate and carry out widespread investigations and potential prosecutions. That Musk might need protecting from a man who has famously turned on him before may give him pause for thought.

The richest man in the world is too wayward a character to adjust quietly to these pressures. But the outcome of this check-in with an electorate disillusioned by Trump – and, indeed, with Musk – and uneasy about the untrammelled power of technology means that he will have to choose more decisively between his role as figure in the ideological debate and his role at the helm of some of America’s most strategic businesses.

Musk is a man who has used his acquisition of the X platform to create Maga-aligned blend of anti-Woke crusades and hot-button broadsides on everything from immigration to the evils of “Woke” progressivism dial that down – the better to focus on forging cross-party support for space exploration, autonomous transport and his role as the key innovator of his generation. The lure of political influence was seductive for a man whose currency is progress and power.

By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection.

W hat’s on your mind right now? You can probably answer this question without thinking too hard about it. Being aware of our own thought processes — a capacity called introspection — seems to come naturally to us.

Yet among philosophers and psychologists, introspection is a subject of active debate. Some think it’s closely related to consciousness . Others argue that it’s an elaborate illusion . It’s tricky to test theories of introspection in the lab — or to pin down a precise definition in the first place.

Now, after over a century of studying introspection in humans and animals, researchers are beginning to explore the phenomenon in unlikely new subjects — large language models. These systems, which are based on mathematical structures called neural networks, excel at cognitive tasks that until recently seemed exclusive to humans. Can they introspect as well?

In 2025, Jack Lindsey , a researcher at Anthropic, devised a way to test introspection in language models by injecting “thoughts” into their neural networks — in a kind of targeted digital neurosurgery. Lindsey’s experiment demonstrated that models could at least sometimes detect and describe these injections . It looked a lot like introspection.

Lindsey’s paper was deliberately limited in scope — it didn’t make broader claims about consciousness. (In particular, it did not imply that language models have subjective first-person experiences .) Even so, it caused a stir online . Researchers rushed to replicate Lindsey’s study with other models.

In the year since, a clearer picture has emerged. Some aspects of the phenomenon Lindsey observed have simpler explanations unrelated to introspection. Others have proved harder to explain away, but whether they should count as introspection remains hotly contested.

Jack Lindsey, a researcher at Anthropic, set out to test whether large language models can “introspect” by subjecting them to a kind of digital neurosurgery.

Courtesy of Jack Lindsey

It’s a heady time for the field, as researchers devise real-world tests for questions that were once considered philosophical. “Given the state of the theoretical landscape, where no one agrees on anything,” Lindsey said, “I think that our best path forward is to do a lot of empirical science.”

Denim, Secrecy, and Vegetables

Language models learn to generate fluent sentences by “training” on vast reams of human-authored text. That means if you ask them what they “think,” their answers may just mimic the kinds of responses found in their training data. “They are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time,” said Shauli Ravfogel , a language model researcher at New York University.

To avoid such pitfalls, researchers want to devise tests of introspection that can’t be gamed using outside information . Ideally, a language model will only pass these tests if it’s actually aware of its current internal state.

Lindsey set out to devise such a test. He’d been a graduate student in computational neuroscience, using neural networks as tools to model brain processes, when the world began to take notice of language models. “It started to feel like there’s just a lot of value in understanding them for their own sake,” he said. In 2024, after receiving his doctorate, he left academia to study the inner workings of language models at Anthropic.

items.content:
How I stopped worrying and learned to love AI. | Koen van Gilst

Skip to main content ← Back to Lab

Sometimes, when all my agents are working and I have a few minutes to reflect, I get this creeping feeling that I'm handing more and more of my work over to AI without really thinking about what I'm giving up.

I wanted to use the generated image above for a conference talk, but I ended up not using it because it didn’t fit the positive and creative message I wanted to communicate. However the image stayed with me, because I like how it captures, in a dramatically fun way, the ambivalence I have about using AI. On the one hand I often feel excited and almost intoxicated by the limitless possibilities AI offers to create any software I can think of.

But in talking about and further enhancing this story of endless new possibilities, I sometimes feel like the mad Dr. Strangelove or the enthusiastic military advisor Buck Turgidson from the Stanley Kubrick film that inspired this image.

It is not just about the mental strain working with AI is putting on all of us. Or the fact that maybe we’re working towards making ourselves redundant. It’s the fact that our software and communication start to feel more mindless. Software is becoming abundant, but also more buggy and vulnerable. Emails become walls of text that nobody wants to read. Presenters are talking about slides they don't fully understand. We’re so enamored by our new smart devices that we’ve given up on thinking things through.

Even so, I’m still excited about AI and this is not an either-or situation. I guess that for the time being, I'm going to have to accept that I can be euphoric, worried and a little crazy at the same time.

To me that's what makes this such an interesting time to be in.

Introducing the FMF Jailbreak Rating Framework for Frontier Cyber Threats

Frontier Model Forum

5th November 2026

Today the Frontier Model Forum (FMF) is releasing Version 1.0 of the FMF’s Jailbreak Rating Framework for Frontier Cyber Threats , a preliminary framework that provides a structured method for rating the comparative risk profile of successful cyber jailbreaks. Our aim is to help build a shared understanding of cyber-related jailbreaks, supporting AI developers, security researchers and policymakers in interpreting and responding to emerging AI-related cyber threats.

As frontier AI models become more capable in the cyber domain, the same capabilities that can help defenders find vulnerabilities and secure systems may also be leveraged by attackers to carry out malicious cyber activity. Managing AI-related cyber risks effectively will require a clear understanding of whether and how model safeguards can be bypassed, and what those failures could enable.

One way model safeguards can be bypassed is through jailbreaks: reproducible techniques that unlock capabilities or information the safeguards are meant to restrict. But not all successful jailbreaks carry the same risks. While some produce model responses of limited practical use, others could give malicious actors access to dangerous cyber capabilities. Without a common method to rate jailbreaks, organizations may assess the same jailbreak differently, struggle to compare findings, and spend limited resources patching lower-risk issues before addressing high-risk threats.

The framework uses a tiered assessment methodology that combines scores across four categories: capability gain, capability scope, ease of deployment, and ease of discovery. It categorizes jailbreaks by the capabilities they unlock and how readily those capabilities can be used, so that assessments are more consistent. The framework is designed to help organizations and teams working to address cyber jailbreaks, ensuring comparability across findings and building a shared understanding of how to prioritize jailbreaks by potential risk.

Hart Rossman, VP of Security at Amazon Web Services said: “ As the security implications of frontier models come into sharper focus, the guardrails that prevent misuse matter more than ever. We’ve long known that guardrail bypasses vary widely in their severity, but until now there hasn’t been an agreed-upon methodology for assessing their impact. The Frontier Model Forum’s new framework gives the industry a shared, evidence-based way to rate how serious a cyber bypass is, so teams can focus on what matters most. Amazon was glad to contribute to the framework’s development, and we look forward to continued collaboration to make AI safer.”

Sarah Heck, Head of Public Affairs at Anthropic said : “Anthropic is pleased to support the work of the FMF to develop a practical, evidence-based framework to manage jailbreak risk. It’s a great example of how industry can work together to ensure AI is deployed safely and securely. I’m grateful to the FMF team and to the security experts across member companies who put this together.”

Owen Larter, Senior Director and Head of Frontier Policy at Google DeepMind said : “This framework provides an important shared approach so that organizations can assess jailbreaks consistently and focus efforts on the highest-risk issues first. We’re glad to have contributed to this initial version and look forward to continuing to work with others in industry, research and government to develop and iterate on best practices.”

Natasha Crampton, VP and Chief Responsible AI Officer at Microsoft said : “The growing cyber capabilities of frontier AI models call for shared approaches to assessing and managing emerging risks. Not all successful jailbreaks pose the same level of risk. The Frontier Model Forum’s new framework lays important groundwork for building shared approaches to identifying the most consequential threats, prioritizing mitigation efforts, and strengthening model safeguards.”

Sasha Baker, Head of National Security Policy at OpenAI said : “As AI models become more capable, we need a consistent way to assess jailbreaks that could enable serious cyber harm. At OpenAI, we’re investing in understanding these risks and strengthening our safeguards–and we’re working across industry to address these challenges. This framework is an important step toward a common methodology for evaluating and comparing the severity of cyber jailbreaks, including the capabilities they unlock and how readily they can be used. Shared approaches like this can help the AI and security communities build a clearer evidence base and prioritize improvements to safeguards.”

BUILDING ON THE FRAMEWORK

Version 1.0 is an initial release. The FMF will continue testing the framework against a range of jailbreaks to see whether different assessors reach similar ratings and whether those ratings reflect meaningful differences in risk. We will also update it as new jailbreaks are discovered, existing jailbreak techniques evolve, and the empirical understanding of jailbreaks matures.

We also look forward to working with the broader ecosystem to improve the framework. To that end, we are opening a public comment period through December 21, 2026. We invite external experts and organizations to submit feedback on the framework to comments@frontiermodelforum.org . We will review the feedback in consultation with our members and incorporate relevant input into an updated version.

The framework is one part of the FMF’s broader effort on AI-cyber risks . Looking ahead, our AI-cyber and security workstreams will continue to focus on strengthening model safeguards, developing methods for assessing frontier cyber capabilities of concern, and building shared approaches that help the ecosystem anticipate and respond to emerging AI-enabled cyber threats.

items.title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
items.summary: Teaching AI to build scientific models（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
01 A three-step program

AI for Science grantees Jakob Macke , Daniel Gedon , and Stefan Wahl are researchers at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the University of Tübingen, where they build AI tools for developing scientific models in neuroscience and beyond. In this guest post, they discuss how AI is starting to change scientific modeling.

In 1951, Cambridge University’s computer went out of action for six months. This was inconvenient for physiologist Andrew Huxley, who, alongside his colleague Alan Hodgkin, had just built a set of equations to describe how a particular squid nerve cell fired. The scientists wanted to understand the “action potential” of these nerve cells: the electrical pulses they use to communicate, which underlie everything brains do, from perception to intelligence. The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data.

Huxley had hoped to use the newfangled computer to solve the equations. Instead, he was forced to solve them using a hand-cranked mechanical calculator. It took him over three weeks.

The basic structure of their model was dictated by known facts about the cell. Hodgkin and Huxley modeled its membrane as an electrical circuit. One part of the model, however, was just an educated guess. In order to make the curve fit the data they had measured, they found that they had to raise one variable to the fourth power—that is, to multiply it by itself three times. At the time, they did not know why. They just knew that otherwise the model didn’t predict the observed data as well.

They did offer a hypothesis, however. They cautiously suggested that the variable in question, which governed how particular gates in the cell membrane opened, might require the fourth power because multiple charged particles in the membrane had to move into place before the gate would open.

Decades later, long after both Hodgkin and Huxley had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963, another team found the structure of a related potassium channel protein . And they discovered that, yes, it had four identical pieces arranged around a central pore . The model was fit to the data in 1951. Even then, it predicted how fast the impulse travels relatively accurately. More than that, it turned out to have helped predict the structure of potassium ion channels themselves, which it had never been fit to.

Today, an AI system could plausibly find an equation like Hodgkin and Huxley’s in an afternoon, and perhaps it would fit the experimental data even more closely. But the point of the story is that simply knowing the fourth power did the job was not enough; what mattered was knowing that a simpler version of the model did not work. An AI system that merely hands you the model might give you an answer, but it does not give you understanding. Reproducing the data with a model is insufficient, because any number of models could do the same. What matters is being able to make claims about the real-world system itself, and ideally about other, similar systems. To do so, you need to know which features the model shares with other models that work, and which set it apart from models that don’t. As the mathematician Richard Hamming wrote in 1962, “The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.”

A three-step program

More than 70 years on, the Hodgkin-Huxley model remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons. The same kinds of equations, with different constants, describe nerve cells across the animal kingdom, from squids to humans, even though our evolutionary lineages separated more than half a billion years ago.

Even more important than its longevity, however, is what the Hodgkin-Huxley model tells us about how models work. Hodgkin and Huxley’s approach can be broken down into three steps, and most scientific modeling involves some version of them.

The first is building the model. This means deciding what the model is made of and what shape its equations take. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s case, that meant the parts of the electrical circuit—the membrane and the gates—and the form of the equations, such as raising the underlying variable to the fourth power.

The second is constraining the model—tuning its adjustable parameters to fit real measurements. For Hodgkin and Huxley, that included settings like how often the gates open under different voltages.

The third is interpreting the model—asking what the model says about the real system, such as suggesting that the fourth power meant the gate had four moving parts.

In practice, scientists go through these steps repeatedly . If the numbers fail to fit the measurements, or if the interpretation makes no sense, they go back and revise.

All three steps were once done by people, but AI systems are increasingly involved in each of them. Machines have arguably made the most progress in constraining models, so we’ll start there.

Splitting the bill, or how to constrain models

When Hodgkin and Huxley constrained their model by eye and intuition, they ended up with a single set of numbers. This told them that the model could match the data. It didn’t tell them whether other numbers would have worked just as well or even better.

Imagine you know that a group dinner added up to $120, but not who ordered what. Many different combinations of orders could have added up to that amount—perhaps everyone ordered a mid-priced burger, or perhaps one person had steak and lobster while everyone else had soup. Models of nerve cells work on the same principle: different combinations of gate parameters can produce near-identical electrical activity. Simply showing one combination that fits well hides all the other plausible parameter settings, and other combinations might have led to different predictions. This is true of almost any phenomenon being modeled. Many different sets of parameters can explain the observed data equally well.

The End of the Internet

Monday, October 26, 2026

It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress.

It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install!

I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable , an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever.

The End of Blogs

2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet ; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom , also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space:

Talking Points Memo , Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000

Instapundit , Little Green Footballs , and Dooce launched in 2001

Matt Yglesias , Daily Kos , Eschaton , The Volokh Conspiracy , Power Line , Gizmodo , Gawker , paidContent , and Daring Fireball launched in 2002

Ezra Klein , Marginal Revolution , ReadWriteWeb , and AVC launched in 2003

That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference.

Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain.

Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business.

For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future :

It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost…

I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone.

In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for.

Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses

Security researchers discovered residential proxy activity on the White House’s network.

Security researchers discovered residential proxy activity on the White House’s network.

by Emma Roth

Nov 6, 2026, 5:40 PM UTC

Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just “a few dollars,” as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register . That’s according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient , which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network.

A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from. Some apps and browser extensions include third-party software development kits (SDKs) that put proxy nodes on a user’s device — whether users know it or not. Third-party services can then sell access to the residential proxies on users’ devices.

As noted by the cybersecurity firm Spur , people can legitimately use residential proxies for purposes like ad verification and quality assurance testing, but bad actors can also use them to bypass geolocation controls and defensive filters. Hackers have used residential proxies for all kinds of malicious activity , including to create botnets and carry out account takeovers .

At the White House, Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services routed traffic out of the network from October 5th to November 3rd. It notes that this activity typically happens between 5PM ET and midnight. “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” Layer3 says. The SDK in question might be linked to the watch party app Rave, according to Synthient, which says the app “bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform.”

Synthient found “a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices on the White House’s network beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica and Mellowtel.” As noted by Krebs on Security , Infatica is a proxy service founded by Vladimir Fomenko, the owner of King Servers, which was linked to 2016 cyberattacks on election systems in Illinois and Arizona.

Layer3 warns that the residential proxy is “public access,” adding that “anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.”

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.

But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.

We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”

It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.

It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.

class="my-2.5 mx-auto px-[15px] sm:px-5 lg:grid lg:max-w-5xl lg:grid-cols-3 lg:gap-6 lg:px-8 xl:px-0">

Specifications and performance

For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.

And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.

The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote . The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.

Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.

class="my-2.5 mx-auto px-[15px] sm:px-5 lg:grid lg:max-w-5xl lg:grid-cols-3 lg:gap-6 lg:px-8 xl:px-0">

Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.

A monster of a display

Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.

Welcome to Edition 9.18 of the Rocket Report! Blue Origin packed a lot of news into one afternoon Thursday with the reveal of a new kick stage for the New Glenn rocket, a new rocket engine design, and the minor and widely expected delay for New Glenn’s return-to-flight mission from December until January. The reconstruction of Blue Origin’s wrecked launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida, continues apace after a catastrophic explosion nearly six months ago. There’s a lot of pent-up demand from NASA, Amazon, and the Space Force for Blue Origin to get New Glenn back in action.

As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

SpaceX vets work on water-fed propulsion . Three brothers who worked at SpaceX in the Falcon 9 era are now building satellites that run on water, a potentially harvestable resource on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, Ars reports . In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space’s satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.

How does this work? … Argo Space flew its first mission in July, but the spacecraft failed after one of its solar arrays didn’t deploy, and there wasn’t enough time to test the propulsion system. Two more missions are on Argo Space’s schedule for 2027 to demonstrate the company’s water-based thrusters. The propulsion system is basically a small rocket that uses hydrogen and oxygen as propellants. However, instead of launching with separate tanks of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the satellite carries a reservoir of liquid water. In space, the vehicle uses solar power to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases and burns them to generate thrust.

JAXA backs small satellite launcher . Japanese launcher startup Interstellar Technologies has secured the backing of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) for its Zero rocket program, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports . The company said JAXA selected it for its Acceleration of Commercial Rocket Launch Demonstration program under the Space Strategic Fund. The government-funded program supports development and flight demonstrations of private launch companies with grants of up to $76 million per company, with the goal of fostering a growing commercial launch industry in Japan. Interstellar previously raised more than $250 million, with roughly equivalent funds from government and private capital.

Zeroing in … Interstellar is using the money to complete development of its Zero rocket, a two-stage launcher designed to carry up to 1 metric ton (2,200 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. “We have achieved critical technical milestones, including Japan’s first successful firing test of an orbital-class methane engine,” said Satoshi Nakayama, director of the board and president of Interstellar. “We have now reached the stage where we must swiftly turn these proven development results into operational commercial services.” The most recent update from Interstellar indicated a first launch of Zero in 2027.

Launch demand outpacing supply . A new report from analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years, Ars reports . The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.
